Core groups

Daniel S. Silver    Lorenzo Traldi    Susan G. Williams
Abstract

The core group of a classical link was introduced independently by A.J. Kelly in 1991 and M. Wada in 1992. It is a link invariant defined by a presentation involving the arcs and crossings of a diagram, related to Wirtinger’s presentation of the fundamental group of a link complement. Two close relatives of the core group are defined by presentations involving regions rather than arcs; one of them is related to Dehn’s presentation of a link group. The definitions are extended to virtual link diagrams and properties of the resulting invariants are discussed.

Keywords: checkerboard coloring, classical link, Dehn presentation, virtual link; AMS Classification: MSC: 57K10

1 Introduction

The core group of a classical link was introduced independently by A.J. Kelly [10] and M. Wada [16]. Although defined combinatorially by a presentation with generators corresponding to the arcs of a diagram of the link, it has a topological interpretation as the free product of an infinite cyclic group and the fundamental group of the 2-fold cover of 𝕊3{\mathbb{S}}^{3} branched over the link [13, 14, 16]. Here we describe two close relatives, each group defined by a presentation obtained from a link diagram but with generators corresponding to the regions of the diagram rather than the arcs. All three groups are defined for virtual link diagrams. The first is an invariant of virtual links while the second and third are invariants for links in thickened surfaces.

We recall some conventional notation and terminology. By a classical link we will mean a knot or link in 3-space. (Later we will consider links in more general 3-manifolds.) A classical link diagram DD is a finite immersed collection of closed curves in the plane whose only (self-)intersections are transverse double points. An intersection is called a (classical) crossing. At a classical crossing one of the segments is designated as the underpasser, while the other is the overpasser. They are indicated by removing a short part of the underpasser. A diagram is oriented if a direction has been assigned to each closed component. Ambient isotopy classes of classical links correspond to equivalence classes of classical link diagrams under classical Reidemeister moves (see, for example, [11]).

A virtual link diagram is a link diagram as above but which may also contain a second type of intersection called a virtual crossing, and indicated by a small circle enclosing it. (A virtual link diagram is not required to have any virtual crossings.) A virtual link is an equivalence class of virtual link diagrams under generalized Reidemeister moves, a finite set of local changes of a diagram that includes Reidemeister moves. The concept is due to L. Kauffman and details can be found in [9]. If two classical link diagrams are equivalent under generalized Reidemeister moves, then they are equivalent under classical Reidemeister moves [7]. Consequently, virtual link theory extends the classical theory. By a virtual link we will mean a classical or virtual link.

We begin with the definition of Kelly and Wada’s core group, which we will call the arc core group. If DD is a virtual link diagram then an arc of DD is a segment that extends in both directions until it arrives at a classical crossing where it is an underpasser. The set of arcs of DD is denoted A⁡(D)A(D), and the set of classical crossings of DD is denoted C⁡(D)C(D).

Definition 1.1.

Let DD be a virtual link diagram, and let {ga∣a∈A⁡(D)}\{g_{a}\mid a\in A(D)\} be a set of symbols in one-to-one correspondence with A⁡(D)A(D). If c∈C⁡(D)c\in C(D) is a classical crossing with overpassing arc a1​(c)a_{1}(c) and underpassing arcs a2​(c)a_{2}(c) and a3​(c)a_{3}(c), let rc=ga1​(c)​ga2​(c)−1​ga1​(c)​ga3​(c)−1r_{c}=g_{a_{1}(c)}g^{-1}_{a_{2}(c)}g_{a_{1}(c)}g^{-1}_{a_{3}(c)}. Then the arc core group A​C​(D)AC(D) is the group with presentation ⟨{ga∣a∈A⁡(D)};{rc∣c∈C⁡(D)}⟩\langle\{g_{a}\mid a\in A(D)\};\{r_{c}\mid c\in C(D)\}\rangle.

The notation A​C​(D)AC(D) is intended to emphasize that the arc core group is defined using A⁡(D)A(D). Notice that A​C​(D)AC(D) is well defined, because the group-theoretic significance of a crossing relator rcr_{c} is not changed if the indices of the underpassing arcs a2​(c),a3​(c)a_{2}(c),a_{3}(c) are interchanged. It is well known (and not difficult to verify) that A​C​(D)AC(D) is invariant under generalized Reidemeister moves. Hence it is a virtual link invariant A​C​(L)AC(L).

The other members of the core group family that we discuss are defined using the regions of a link diagram, rather than the arcs. For a classical link diagram DD, the regions are defined to be the connected components of the complement in the plane of the union of immersed circles from which DD is built. For a virtual link diagram DD, the regions are defined to be the connected components of the complement of the union of immersed circles in the abstract link diagram standardly associated with DD [8]. An abstract link diagram is a compact orientable surface that has as a deformation retraction the underlying 4-valent graph of DD, with vertices corresponding to classical crossings (and virtual crossings ignored).

For a classical link diagram, the classical and virtual notions of “regions” are not the same. There are two reasons for this disparity.

(1.) Recall that a link diagram DD is split if there is an embedded circle in the plane with nonempty parts of DD both inside and outside. The abstract link diagram associated with a split diagram DD is the disjoint union of the abstract link diagrams associated with the non-split subdiagrams whose split union is DD. Therefore no two of these subdiagrams share any region. However, if DD is a split classical diagram considered in the plane, then the non-split subdiagrams that constitute DD are connected to each other by shared complementary regions. As a result, if DD is the split union of kk disjoint non-split subdiagrams, then DD will have k−1k-1 fewer regions according to the classical definition than it has according to the virtual definition.

(2.) Even for a non-split classical diagram, there is a difference between the classical regions (the bounded regions are disks) and the virtual regions (which are annuli). This difference has no significance in our discussion, as there is a natural correspondence between the classical regions and the virtual regions.

The disparity between the classical and virtual notions of “regions” is reflected in the following.

Definition 1.2.

If DD is a classical link diagram then R⁡(D)R(D) denotes the set of regions of DD according to the classical definition, and Rv​(D)R_{v}(D) denotes the set of regions of DD according to the virtual definition. If DD is a non-classical virtual link diagram, then R⁡(D)R(D) denotes the set of regions of DD according to the virtual definition.

Definition 1.3.

Let DD be a virtual link diagram, let R⁡(D)R(D) be the set of regions of DD, and let {γR∣R∈R⁡(D)}\{{\gamma}_{R}\mid R\in R(D)\} be a set of symbols in one-to-one correspondence with R⁡(D)R(D). If c∈C⁡(D)c\in C(D) is a classical crossing as pictured in Figure 1, let ρc=γV​γW−1​γY​γX−1{\rho}_{c}={\gamma}_{V}{\gamma}^{-1}_{W}{\gamma}_{Y}{\gamma}^{-1}_{X}. Then the first regional core group R​C​(D)RC(D) is the group with presentation ⟨{γR∣R∈R⁡(D)};{ρc∣c∈C⁡(D)}⟩\langle\{{\gamma}_{R}\mid R\in R(D)\};\{{\rho}_{c}\mid c\in C(D)\}\rangle.

The significance of a relator rr in a group presentation is unchanged if rr is replaced by its inverse, or if the terms in rr or r−1r^{-1} are cyclically permuted. It follows that if cc is the crossing pictured in Figure 1, then the significance of ρc{\rho}_{c} is unchanged if the regions are relabeled as follows: VV is any one of the four regions; WW is the region across the overpassing arc from VV; XX is the region diagonally across the crossing from VV; and YY is the region across an underpassing arc from VV.

In Section 2 we prove:

Theorem 1.4.

If DD is a classical link diagram, then R​C​(D)RC(D) is isomorphic to the free product ℤ∗A​C​(D)\mathbb{Z}*AC(D).

Our second regional core group is defined using the following notion of crossing index.

Definition 1.5.

If cc is a classical crossing as illustrated in Figure 1, then the crossing indices of cc are ηc​(V,X)=ηc​(X,V)=−1\eta_{c}(V,X)=\eta_{c}(X,V)=-1 and ηc​(W,Y)=ηc​(Y,W)=1\eta_{c}(W,Y)=\eta_{c}(Y,W)=1.

Definition 1.6.

Let DD be a virtual link diagram, and let {gR∣R∈R⁡(D)}\{g_{R}\mid R\in R(D)\} be a set of symbols in one-to-one correspondence with R⁡(D)R(D). rR=∏i=1k(gR−1​gQi)ηci​(R,Qi).r_{R}=\prod_{i=1}^{k}(g^{-1}_{R}g_{Q_{i}})^{\eta_{c_{i}}(R,Q_{i})}.
Theorem 1.7.

Let DD be a classical link diagram that is the split union of kk disjoint non-split diagrams, and let Fk+1F_{k+1} be a free group of rank k+1k+1. Then the free products R​C​(D)∗R​C​(D)RC(D)*RC(D) and Fk+1∗R​R​C​(D)F_{k+1}*RRC(D) are isomorphic.

Theorems 1.4 and 1.7 imply that for non-split classical link diagrams, any one of the three groups A​C​(D),R​C​(D),R​R​C​(D)AC(D),RC(D),RRC(D) determines the other two. The situation for virtual diagrams is quite different: in general no two of the groups determine the third. See Figure 2 for examples.

Recall that two virtual link diagrams are equivalent if one can be transformed into the other through some finite sequence of detour moves (which involve only virtual crossings) and Reidemeister moves Ω​.1,Ω​.2,Ω​.3\Omega.1,\Omega.2,\Omega.3 (which involve only classical crossings). The groups A​C​(D),R​C​(D)AC(D),RC(D) and R​R​C​(D)RRC(D) are all invariant under Ω​.1\Omega.1 and Ω​.3\Omega.3 moves, and also under detour moves. For classical diagrams, A​C​(D)AC(D) and R​C​(D)RC(D) are invariant under Ω​.2\Omega.2 moves, and if DD is the split union of kk non-split diagrams, then Fk+1∗R​R​C​(D)F_{k+1}*RRC(D) is invariant under Ω​.2\Omega.2 moves.

For virtual link diagrams DD, the group A​C​(D)AC(D) remains invariant under Ω​.2\Omega.2 moves, but the regional groups are not invariant. Nevertheless, R​C​(D)RC(D) and R​R​C​(D)RRC(D) provide invariants of links in thickened surfaces. See Sections 4 and 9.

2 Proof of Theorem 1.4

We recall that a virtual link diagram DD is checkerboard colorable if it is possible to shade its regions in such a way that at every non-crossing point of an arc aa of DD, there is a shaded region on one side of aa and an unshaded region on the other side of aa. All classical diagrams are checkerboard colorable.

Proposition 2.1.

If DD is a checkerboard colorable virtual link diagram, then there is a function f:A⁡(D)→R​C​(D)f:A(D)\to RC(D) defined as follows: If a∈A⁡(D)a\in A(D) has a shaded region SS on one side and an unshaded region UU on the other side, then f⁡(a)=γU​γS−1f(a)={\gamma}_{U}{\gamma}^{-1}_{S}.

Proof.

Well-definedness of ff requires that if cc is a crossing with overpassing arc aa, then we have the same value for γU​γS−1{\gamma}_{U}{\gamma}^{-1}_{S} on both sides of cc.

Suppose that aa is the overpassing arc at the crossing cc pictured in Figure 1. If the shaded regions are WW and YY then γU​γS−1=γV​γW−1{\gamma}_{U}{\gamma}^{-1}_{S}={\gamma}_{V}{\gamma}^{-1}_{W} on one side of cc, and γU​γS−1=γX​γY−1{\gamma}_{U}{\gamma}^{-1}_{S}={\gamma}_{X}{\gamma}^{-1}_{Y} on the other side of cc. The crossing relator γV​γW−1​γY​γX−1{\gamma}_{V}{\gamma}^{-1}_{W}{\gamma}_{Y}{\gamma}^{-1}_{X} tells us that γV​γW−1=γX​γY−1{\gamma}_{V}{\gamma}^{-1}_{W}={\gamma}_{X}{\gamma}^{-1}_{Y}. Similarly, if the shaded regions are VV and XX then γU​γS−1=γW​γV−1{\gamma}_{U}{\gamma}^{-1}_{S}={\gamma}_{W}{\gamma}^{-1}_{V} on one side of cc, and γU​γS−1=γY​γX−1{\gamma}_{U}{\gamma}^{-1}_{S}={\gamma}_{Y}{\gamma}^{-1}_{X} on the other side of cc. The crossing relator γV​γW−1​γY​γX−1{\gamma}_{V}{\gamma}^{-1}_{W}{\gamma}_{Y}{\gamma}^{-1}_{X} tells us that γW​γV−1=γY​γX−1{\gamma}_{W}{\gamma}^{-1}_{V}={\gamma}_{Y}{\gamma}^{-1}_{X}. ∎

Following the path P⁡(U)P(U) from S0S_{0} to UU provides a sequence S0,a0,U0,b0,S1,a1,U1,…,ak,Uk=US_{0},a_{0},U_{0},b_{0},S_{1},a_{1},U_{1},\dots,a_{k},U_{k}=U such that every SiS_{i} is a shaded region of DD, every UiU_{i} is an unshaded region of DD, every aia_{i} is an arc of DD with SiS_{i} on one side and UiU_{i} on the other side, and every bib_{i} is an arc of DD with UiU_{i} on one side and Si+1S_{i+1} on the other side. Denote this sequence W​P​(U)WP(U), and let h⁡(W​P​(U))=gak​gbk−1−1​…​gb0−1​ga0∈A​C​(D)h(WP(U))=g_{a_{k}}g^{-1}_{b_{k-1}}\dots g^{-1}_{b_{0}}g_{a_{0}}\in AC(D). The same kind of argument given above shows that h⁡(W​P​(U))h(WP(U)) does not depend on the choice of the path P⁡(U)P(U).

We now have a well-defined function h:R⁡(D)→A​C​(D)h:R(D)\to AC(D). To verify that hh defines a homomorphism R​C​(D)→A​C​(D)RC(D)\to AC(D), suppose cc is a crossing as pictured in Figure 1. In the introduction we mentioned that the choice of region labels V,W,X,YV,W,X,Y in Figure 1 is quite flexible; VV can be any one of the four regions, so long as WW neighbors VV across the overpassing arc and YY neighbors VV across an underpassing arc. We may assume that the path P⁡(W)P(W) is obtained by first following P⁡(V)P(V), and then crossing aa from VV to WW. Then

h⁡(W​P​(V))​h​(W​P​(W))−1=(gak​gbk−1−1​…​gb0−1​ga0)​(ga−1​gak​gbk−1−1​…​gb0−1​ga0)−1=ga.h(WP(V))h(WP(W))^{-1}=(g_{a_{k}}g^{-1}_{b_{k-1}}\dots g^{-1}_{b_{0}}g_{a_{0}})(g^{-1}_{a}g_{a_{k}}g^{-1}_{b_{k-1}}\dots g^{-1}_{b_{0}}g_{a_{0}})^{-1}=g_{a}.

A similar calculation shows that h⁡(W​P​(X))​h​(W​P​(Y))−1=gah(WP(X))h(WP(Y))^{-1}=g_{a} too. Then

h⁡(W​P​(V))​h​(W​P​(W))−1​h​(W​P​(Y))​h​(W​P​(X))−1=ga​ga−1=1​,h(WP(V))h(WP(W))^{-1}h(WP(Y))h(WP(X))^{-1}=g_{a}g^{-1}_{a}=1\text{,}

so the image under hh of the crossing relator ρc=γV​γW−1​γY​γX−1{\rho}_{c}={\gamma}_{V}{\gamma}^{-1}_{W}{\gamma}_{Y}{\gamma}^{-1}_{X} is trivial. It follows that γR↦h⁡(W​P​(R)CLOSE{\gamma}_{R}\mapsto h(WP(R) defines a homomorphism R​C​(D)→A​C​(D)RC(D)\to AC(D), which we also denote hh.

To complete the proof, we need to show that if a∈A⁡(D)a\in A(D) then h⁡(f⁡(ga))=gah(f(g_{a}))=g_{a}. The argument is the same as the calculation of h⁡(W​P​(V))​h​(W​P​(W))−1=gah(WP(V))h(WP(W))^{-1}=g_{a} in the preceding paragraph. ∎

3 Proof of Theorem 1.7

Before beginning the proof, observe that if DD is a checkerboard colorable link diagram, then for each region R∈R⁡(D)R\in R(D), the relator rRr_{R} of Definition 1.6 involves only generators corresponding to regions with the same shaded/unshaded status as RR itself. It follows that the group R​R​C​(D)RRC(D) is the internal free product R​R​C​(D)=R​R​CS​(D)∗R​R​CU​(D)RRC(D)=RRC_{S}(D)*RRC_{U}(D), where the subgroup R​R​CS​(D)RRC_{S}(D) corresponds to the shaded regions and the subgroup R​R​CU​(D)RRC_{U}(D) corresponds to the unshaded regions.

Now, let DD be a classical link diagram. There is a shaded checkerboard graph Γs​(D)\Gamma_{s}(D), with a vertex for each shaded region and an edge for each crossing; the edge corresponding to the crossing cc is incident on the vertex or vertices corresponding to shaded region(s) incident at cc. There is also an unshaded checkerboard graph Γu​(D)\Gamma_{u}(D), with vertices for the unshaded regions of DD and edges for crossings of DD, defined in the same way. We use βs​(D)\beta_{s}(D) to denote the number of connected components of Γs​(D)\Gamma_{s}(D), and βu​(D)\beta_{u}(D) to denote the number of connected components of Γu​(D)\Gamma_{u}(D).

We can eliminate most of the generators of R​C​(D)RC(D) corresponding to shaded regions, as follows. Choose shaded regions S1,…,Sβs​(D)S_{1},\dots,S_{\beta_{s}(D)}, one in each connected component of the graph Γs​(D)\Gamma_{s}(D). Suppose SS is a shaded region that is in the same connected component of Γs​(D)\Gamma_{s}(D) as SnS_{n}, but is not equal to SnS_{n}. Then there is a path P⁡(S)P(S) from SnS_{n} to SS in the plane, which avoids the unshaded regions of DD. Say P⁡(S)P(S) is Sn=Σ0,c1,Σ1,…,ck,Σk=SS_{n}=\Sigma_{0},c_{1},\Sigma_{1},\dots,c_{k},\Sigma_{k}=S, where each Σi\Sigma_{i} is a shaded region and each cic_{i} is a crossing. For 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k let UiU_{i} be the unshaded region on the left of cic_{i} (as seen by an observer standing in Σi\Sigma_{i} and facing Σi+1\Sigma_{i+1}), let ViV_{i} be the unshaded region on the right, and let ηi=ηci​(Ui,Vi)\eta_{i}=\eta_{c_{i}}(U_{i},V_{i}) according to Definition 1.5. Also, let

γ⁡(P⁡(S))=∏i=1k(γUi−1​γVi)ηi.{\gamma}(P(S))=\prod_{i=1}^{k}({\gamma}^{-1}_{U_{i}}{\gamma}_{V_{i}})^{\eta_{i}}.

According to Definition 1.3, γΣi​γUi−1​γVi​γΣi+1−1=1{\gamma}_{\Sigma_{i}}{\gamma}^{-1}_{U_{i}}{\gamma}_{V_{i}}{\gamma}^{-1}_{\Sigma_{i+1}}=1 if ηi=1\eta_{i}=1, and γUi​γΣi+1−1​γΣi​γVi−1=1{\gamma}_{U_{i}}{\gamma}^{-1}_{\Sigma_{i+1}}{\gamma}_{\Sigma_{i}}{\gamma}^{-1}_{V_{i}}=1 if ηi=−1\eta_{i}=-1. Either way,

γΣi−1​γΣi+1=(γUi−1​γVi)ηi.{\gamma}^{-1}_{\Sigma_{i}}{\gamma}_{\Sigma_{i+1}}=({\gamma}^{-1}_{U_{i}}{\gamma}_{V_{i}})^{\eta_{i}}.

It follows that

γS=γΣ0​γΣ0−1​γΣ1​γΣ1−1​γΣ2​…​γΣk−1−1​γΣk=γSn⋅∏i=1k(γUi−1​γVi)ηi=γSn⋅γ⁡(P⁡(S)).{\gamma}_{S}={\gamma}_{\Sigma_{0}}{\gamma}^{-1}_{\Sigma_{0}}{\gamma}_{\Sigma_{1}}{\gamma}^{-1}_{\Sigma_{1}}{\gamma}_{\Sigma_{2}}\dots{\gamma}^{-1}_{\Sigma_{k-1}}{\gamma}_{\Sigma_{k}}={\gamma}_{S_{n}}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{k}({\gamma}^{-1}_{U_{i}}{\gamma}_{V_{i}})^{\eta_{i}}={\gamma}_{S_{n}}\cdot{\gamma}(P(S)).

If we use these relations γS=γSn⋅γ⁡(P⁡(S)){\gamma}_{S}={\gamma}_{S_{n}}\cdot{\gamma}(P(S)) to eliminate every generator γS{\gamma}_{S} with S∉{S1,…,SOPENβs​(D))}S\notin\{S_{1},\dots,\allowbreak S_{\beta_{s}(D))}\}, then we will be left with a presentation of R​C​(D)RC(D) that has generators from the set {γU∣U​ is an unshaded region of ​D}∪{γS1,…,γSOPENβs​(D))}\{{\gamma}_{U}\mid U\text{ is an unshaded region of }D\}\cup\{{\gamma}_{S_{1}},\dots,{\gamma}_{S_{\beta_{s}(D))}}\}, and has relations stating that whenever P⁡(S)P(S) and P′​(S)P^{\prime}(S) are paths from an SnS_{n} to the same unshaded region SS, γ⁡(P⁡(S))=γ⁡(P′​(S)){\gamma}(P(S))={\gamma}(P^{\prime}(S)). Notice that the generators γSn{\gamma}_{S_{n}} do not appear in any of these relations.

The relations γ⁡(P⁡(S))=γ⁡(P′​(S)){\gamma}(P(S))={\gamma}(P^{\prime}(S)) may be equivalently described this way: γ⁡(P)=1{\gamma}(P)=1 whenever PP is a closed path in Γs​(D)\Gamma_{s}(D) that begins and ends in SnS_{n}. Notice that this relationship between P1P_{1} and P3P_{3} implies that when a crossing is traversed as part of P3P_{3}, ηi\eta_{i} remains the same but the regions denoted UiU_{i} and ViV_{i} are interchanged. so as a relator, γ⁡(P){\gamma}(P) is equivalent to γ⁡(P2){\gamma}(P_{2}), which is the same as the relator rUr_{U} of Definition 1.6.

Putting all of this together, we obtain an isomorphism

R​C​(D)≅R​R​CU​(D)∗Fβs​(D).RC(D)\cong RRC_{U}(D)*F_{\beta_{s}(D)}.

Combining the two isomorphisms, we have

R​C​(D)∗R​C​(D)≅R​R​CU​(D)∗R​R​CS​(D)∗Fβs​(D)+βu​(D).RC(D)*RC(D)\cong RRC_{U}(D)*RRC_{S}(D)*F_{\beta_{s}(D)+\beta_{u}(D)}.

Theorem 1.7 follows, because R​R​CU​(D)∗R​R​CS​(D)≅R​R​C​(D)RRC_{U}(D)*RRC_{S}(D)\cong RRC(D) and if DD is the split union of kk non-split diagrams, then βs​(D)+βu​(D)=k+1\beta_{s}(D)+\beta_{u}(D)=k+1.

Remark 3.1.

In [15] it is shown that if LL is a classical link with Goeritz matrix GG, and 𝟎\bf 0 denotes a zero matrix with βs​(D)\beta_{s}(D) columns, then there is a rewritten version of the Dehn presentation of π1​(𝕊3−L)\pi_{1}({\mathbb{S}}^{3}-L) that yields the matrix (G𝟎)\begin{pmatrix}G&\bf 0\end{pmatrix} through Fox’s free differential calculus. Here the algebra is not so complicated, as the free differential calculus is not required: the natural presentation of R​R​CU​(D)∗Fβs​(D)RRC_{U}(D)*F_{\beta_{s}(D)} yields (G𝟎)\begin{pmatrix}G&\bf 0\end{pmatrix} through simple abelianization.

4 Reidemeister moves

We leave the rather mechanical proofs of Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 to the reader.

Proposition 4.1.

For any virtual link diagram DD, the arc core group A​C​(D)AC(D) is invariant under detour moves and Reidemeister moves. That is, A​C​(D)AC(D) is an invariant of virtual link type.

Proposition 4.2.

For any virtual link diagram DD, the region core groups R​C​(D)RC(D) and R​R​C​(D)RRC(D) are invariant under detour moves and Reidemeister moves of types Ω​.1\Omega.1 and Ω​.3\Omega.3.

For classical link diagrams, Theorem 1.4 implies that R​C​(D)RC(D) is invariant under all Ω​.2\Omega.2 moves, and Theorem 1.7 implies that R​R​C​(D)RRC(D) is invariant under Ω​.2\Omega.2 moves that do not change the number kk of non-split pieces of DD. In contrast, an Ω​.2\Omega.2 move on a virtual link diagram can change R​C​(D)RC(D), or change R​R​C​(D)RRC(D) without changing the number kk. See Figure 3 for some examples.

The following proposition shows that some Ω​.2\Omega.2 moves on virtual link diagrams do preserve R​C​(D)RC(D) and R​R​C​(D)RRC(D).

Proposition 4.3.

Consider the Ω​.2\Omega.2 move pictured in Figure 4.

  • •

    If γX=γY{\gamma}_{X}={\gamma}_{Y} in R​C​(D)RC(D), then R​C​(D)≅R​C​(D′)RC(D)\cong RC(D^{\prime}).

  • •

    If AA and CC are distinct regions in D′D^{\prime}, then R​R​C​(D)≅R​R​C​(D′)RRC(D)\cong RRC(D^{\prime}).

Proof.

Notice that the left-hand sides of AA and CC in D′D^{\prime} come from the region XX of DD, and the right-hand sides of AA and CC come from YY.

Relations in R​C​(D′)RC(D^{\prime}) include γZ​γA−1=γW​γB−1{\gamma}_{Z}{\gamma}_{A}^{-1}={\gamma}_{W}{\gamma}_{B}^{-1} and γW​γB−1=γZ​γC−1{\gamma}_{W}{\gamma}_{B}^{-1}={\gamma}_{Z}{\gamma}_{C}^{-1}, implying γA=γC{\gamma}_{A}={\gamma}_{C} in R​C​(D′)RC(D^{\prime}). If γX=γY{\gamma}_{X}={\gamma}_{Y} in R​C​(D)RC(D), then there is a well-defined isomorphism f:R​C​(D)→R​C​(D′)f:RC(D)\to RC(D^{\prime}) with f⁡(γX)=γA,f⁡(γW)=γW,f⁡(γZ)=γZf({\gamma}_{X})={\gamma}_{A},f({\gamma}_{W})={\gamma}_{W},f({\gamma}_{Z})={\gamma}_{Z}, and f⁡(γR)=γRf({\gamma}_{R})={\gamma}_{R} for every region RR outside the figure.

Relations in R​R​C​(D′)RRC(D^{\prime}) include 1=rB=(gB−1​gA)−1​(gB−1​gC)1=r_{B}=(g^{-1}_{B}g_{A})^{-1}(g^{-1}_{B}g_{C}), implying gA=gCg_{A}=g_{C} in R​R​C​(D′)RRC(D^{\prime}). If AA and CC are distinct regions in D′D^{\prime} then XX and YY are the same region in DD: the left-hand sides of XX are connected to the right-hand sides of YY through AA on the top, and CC on the bottom. The relators rAr_{A} and rCr_{C} are wA​(gA−1​gB)−1w_{A}(g^{-1}_{A}g_{B})^{-1} and wC​gC−1​gBw_{C}g^{-1}_{C}g_{B}, where wAw_{A} and wBw_{B} are words arising from the portions of the boundaries of AA and CC outside the diagram. These relators are equivalent to the equalities gB=gA​wAg_{B}=g_{A}w_{A} and gB=gC​wC−1g_{B}=g_{C}w^{-1}_{C}. Using either equality to eliminate the generator gBg_{B}, we are left with the equality gA​wA=gC​wC−1g_{A}w_{A}=g_{C}w^{-1}_{C}, or equivalently, wA​wC=1w_{A}w_{C}=1. As X=YX=Y, wA​wCw_{A}w_{C} is the same as the relator rXr_{X} of R​R​C​(D)RRC(D). ∎

If DD is a classical link diagram, then Proposition 4.3 includes properties of R​C​(D)RC(D) and R​R​C​(D)RRC(D) that have already been mentioned. On the one hand, XX and YY are the same region on the left-hand side of Figure 4, so the hypothesis γX=γY{\gamma}_{X}={\gamma}_{Y} of Proposition 4.3 is satisfied automatically; thus R​C​(D)RC(D) is invariant under arbitrary Ω​.2\Omega.2 moves. On the other hand, if the two pictured sides of DD are not split from each other, then the two regions AA and CC of D′D^{\prime} cannot be the same, so the hypothesis A≠CA\neq C of Proposition 4.3 is satisfied automatically; thus R​R​C​(D)RRC(D) is invariant under Ω​.2\Omega.2 moves that do not change the number of split pieces of a diagram.

5 Abelianized core groups

In this section we mention some simple properties of the abelianizations of A​C​(D),R​C​(D)AC(D),RC(D) and R​R​C​(D)RRC(D). In general, if GG is a group we use Ga​bG_{ab} to denote the abelianization of GG.

Proposition 5.1.

If AA is an infinite, finitely generated abelian group then A≅A​C​(D)a​bA\cong AC(D)_{ab} for some classical link diagram DD.

Proof.

For any link diagram DD, there is an epimorphism A​C​(D)→ℤAC(D)\to\mathbb{Z} with ga↦1​∀a∈A⁡(D)g_{a}\mapsto 1\thickspace\allowbreak\forall a\in A(D). It follows that A​C​(D)a​bAC(D)_{ab} is infinite.

The reader can easily verify that if DD is a classical link diagram, m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} and D′D^{\prime} is the connected sum of DD with the (2,m)(2,m) torus link diagram pictured in Figure 5, then A​C​(D′)a​b≅A​C​(D)a​b⊕ℤmAC(D^{\prime})_{ab}\cong AC(D)_{ab}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{m}. If AA is an infinite, finitely generated abelian group, then

A≅ℤp⊕ℤm1⊕⋯⊕ℤmqA\cong\mathbb{Z}^{p}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{m_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{m_{q}}

for some choice of integers p≥1p\geq 1, q≥0q\geq 0 and m1,…,mq≥2m_{1},\dots,m_{q}\geq 2. We can construct a classical link diagram DD with A​C​(D)a​b≅AAC(D)_{ab}\cong A by starting with pp disjoint circles, and then taking connected sums with torus links of types (2,m1),…,(2,mq)(2,m_{1}),\dots,(2,m_{q}).∎

Proposition 5.2.

Let DD be a diagram of a μ\mu-component link. Then the 2-rank of A​C​(D)a​bAC(D)_{ab} is μ\mu.

Proof.

The abelian version of the crossing relation 1=ga1​(c)​ga2​(c)−1​ga1​(c)​ga3​(c)−11=g_{a_{1}(c)}g^{-1}_{a_{2}(c)}g_{a_{1}(c)}g^{-1}_{a_{3}(c)} of Definition 1.1 is 1=ga1​(c)2​ga2​(c)−1​ga3​(c)−11=g^{2}_{a_{1}(c)}g^{-1}_{a_{2}(c)}g^{-1}_{a_{3}(c)}. If we reduce exponents modulo 2 we obtain 1=ga2​(c)−1​ga3​(c)−11=g^{-1}_{a_{2}(c)}g^{-1}_{a_{3}(c)}, which is equivalent to ga2​(c)=ga3​(c)g_{a_{2}(c)}=g_{a_{3}(c)}. That is, the quotient group A​C​(D)a​b/(2⋅A​C​(D)a​b)AC(D)_{ab}/(2\cdot AC(D)_{ab}) has a generator for each arc of DD, with relations that imply that at each crossing, the generators corresponding to the two underpassing arcs are equal. It follows that for each component of the link that appears in the diagram, all the generators of A​C​(D)a​b/(2⋅A​C​(D)a​b)AC(D)_{ab}/(2\cdot AC(D)_{ab}) corresponding to arcs of that component are equal. ∎

Notice that Theorems 1.4 and 1.7 imply that for a classical link diagram DD, if TT is the torsion subgroup of A​C​(D)a​bAC(D)_{ab} then TT and T⊕TT\oplus T are isomorphic to the torsion subgroups of R​C​(D)a​bRC(D)_{ab} and R​R​C​(D)a​bRRC(D)_{ab}, respectively. The examples in Figure 2 imply that in contrast, for virtuals the three torsion groups are independent.

6 Another description of A​C​(D)AC(D)

In this section we discuss the fact that in addition to Definition 1.1, the arc core group A​C​(D)AC(D) has another, somewhat more complicated description. Our discussion is modified from J. Przytycki’s account [13].

Let DD be an oriented virtual link diagram, D+D^{+} the diagram obtained by adjoining an unknotted circle with no crossings. Let FA⁡(D+)F_{A(D^{+})} be the free group on the set {xa∣a∈A⁡(D+)}\{x_{a}\mid a\in A(D^{+})\}, and let FA⁡(D+)(2)F_{A(D^{+})}^{(2)} be the subset of FA⁡(D+)F_{A(D^{+})} consisting of elements ∏xaini\prod x_{a_{i}}^{n_{i}} such that ∑ni\sum n_{i} is even. The sum ∑ni\sum n_{i} is not changed by conjugation, so FA⁡(D+)(2)F_{A(D^{+})}^{(2)} is a normal subgroup of FA⁡(D+)F_{A(D^{+})}. Let NN be the normal subgroup of FA⁡(D+)(2)F_{A(D^{+})}^{(2)} generated by {xa2∣a∈A⁡(D+)}\{x^{2}_{a}\mid a\in A(D^{+})\}.

For each crossing c∈C⁡(D)c\in C(D), let a1​(c)a_{1}(c) be the overpassing arc at cc and a2​(c),a3​(c)a_{2}(c),a_{3}(c) the underpassing arcs at cc, labeled in such a way that an observer standing on cc facing forward along a1​(c)a_{1}(c) has a2​(c)a_{2}(c) on the right. The Wirtinger relator w⁡(c)w(c) is then w⁡(c)=xa1​(c)​xa2​(c)​xa1​(c)−1​xa3​(c)−1w(c)=x_{a_{1}(c)}x_{a_{2}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{1}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{3}(c)}. Let W^\widehat{W} be the normal subgroup of FA⁡(D+)(2)/NF_{A(D^{+})}^{(2)}/N generated by {w⁡(c)​N∣c∈C⁡(D)}\{w(c)N\mid c\in C(D)\}.

Lemma 6.1.

NN is a normal subgroup of FA⁡(D+)F_{A(D^{+})}, and W^\widehat{W} is a normal subgroup of FA⁡(D+)/NF_{A(D^{+})}/N.

Proof.

To show that NN is normal in FA⁡(D+)F_{A(D^{+})}, it suffices to show that for every choice of a,b∈A⁡(D+)a,b\in A(D^{+}), xb​xa2​xb−1x_{b}x_{a}^{2}x^{-1}_{b} and xb−1​xa2​xbx^{-1}_{b}x^{2}_{a}x_{b} are both elements of NN. As xb​xa2​xb−1=(xb​xa)​xa2​(xb​xa)−1x_{b}x^{2}_{a}x^{-1}_{b}=(x_{b}x_{a})x^{2}_{a}(x_{b}x_{a})^{-1} and xb−1​xa2​xb=(xa​xb)−1​xa2​(xa​xb)x^{-1}_{b}x^{2}_{a}x_{b}=(x_{a}x_{b})^{-1}x^{2}_{a}(x_{a}x_{b}), xb​xa2​xb−1x_{b}x^{2}_{a}x^{-1}_{b} and xb−1​xa2​xbx^{-1}_{b}x^{2}_{a}x_{b} are both equal to conjugates of xa2x^{2}_{a} by elements of FA⁡(D+)(2)F_{A(D^{+})}^{(2)}. As NN is normal in FA⁡(D+)(2)F_{A(D^{+})}^{(2)}, it follows that xb​xa2​xb−1x_{b}x^{2}_{a}x^{-1}_{b} and xb−1​xa2​xbx^{-1}_{b}x^{2}_{a}x_{b} are both elements of NN.

Similarly, to show that W^\widehat{W} is normal in FA⁡(D+)/NF_{A(D^{+})}/N we must show that for every choice of b∈A⁡(D+)b\in A(D^{+}) and c∈C⁡(D)c\in C(D), xb​w​(c)​xb−1​Nx_{b}w(c)x^{-1}_{b}N and xb−1​w​(c)​xb​Nx^{-1}_{b}w(c)x_{b}N are both elements of W^\widehat{W}. We begin to verify this by observing that

w​(c)−1​N=xa3​(c)​xa1​(c)​xa2​(c)−1​xa1​(c)−1​N=xa3​(c)2​xa3​(c)−1​xa1​(c)​xa2​(c)−2​xa2​(c)​xa1​(c)−1​Nw(c)^{-1}N=x_{a_{3}(c)}x_{a_{1}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{2}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{1}(c)}N=x^{2}_{a_{3}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{3}(c)}x_{a_{1}(c)}x^{-2}_{a_{2}(c)}x_{a_{2}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{1}(c)}N
=xa3​(c)2​N⋅xa3​(c)−1​xa1​(c)​N⋅xa2​(c)−2​N⋅xa2​(c)​xa1​(c)−1​N=x^{2}_{a_{3}(c)}N\cdot x^{-1}_{a_{3}(c)}x_{a_{1}(c)}N\cdot x^{-2}_{a_{2}(c)}N\cdot x_{a_{2}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{1}(c)}N

7 Core group functor

It is well known that the arc core group of a classical link is related to its Wirtinger group. One might anticipate a similar connection between the region core group and the Dehn group. We will explain both relationships, extending the first to the virtual case.

We recall that the Wirtinger group πw​i​r​t​(D)\pi_{wirt}(D) of an oriented virtual link diagram DD has a presentation with generators corresponding to the arcs of DD. Relators correspond to each classical crossing cc as follows: if a1​(c)a_{1}(c) is the overpassing arc at cc and a2​(c),a3​(c)a_{2}(c),a_{3}(c) the underpassing arcs at cc, labeled in such a way that an observer standing on cc facing forward along a1​(c)a_{1}(c) has a2​(c)a_{2}(c) on the right, then the Wirtinger relator corresponding to cc is xa1​(c)​xa2​(c)​xa1​(c)−1​xa3​(c)−1x_{a_{1}(c)}x_{a_{2}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{1}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{3}(c)}. The choice of orientations of the components of DD does not affect πw​i​r​t​(D)\pi_{wirt}(D). It is well known that πw​i​r​t​(D)\pi_{wirt}(D) is invariant under virtual Reidemeister moves, and hence it is an invariant πw​i​r​t​(L)\pi_{wirt}(L) of the virtual link LL described by DD.

The Dehn group πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) is another group that can be associated to DD, although no orientation is necessary. It has a presentation with generators corresponding to the regions of DD, with one generator set equal to the identity, and relators at each crossing of the form χV​χW−1​χX​χY−1\chi_{V}\chi_{W}^{-1}\chi_{X}\chi_{Y}^{-1}, as in Figure 1.

Remark 7.1.

(1.) It is well known that when LL is a classical link, the Wirtinger and Dehn groups are both isomorphic to the fundamental group of the link complement ℝ3∖L\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus L. Although the Wirtinger group is also a virtual link invariant, the Dehn group is not.

(2.) If LL is regarded as a link in a thickened surface, then both πw​i​r​t​(D)\pi_{wirt}(D) and πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) are isotopy invariants. (The proof as in the classical case, using Reidemeister moves, extends.) However, the groups are in general no longer isomorphic. In fact, πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) is a quotient of πw​i​r​t​(D)\pi_{wirt}(D) by a normal subgroup that is easy to describe. We review this below.

(3.) It is a result of [4] that any finitely presented group arises as the Dehn group of some virtual link.

Let GG be a finitely presented group, S⊂GS\subset G a finite subset and NN the normal closure of {s2|s∈S}\{s^{2}|s\in S\}. Assume that ρ:G→ℤ2\rho:G\to\mathbb{Z}_{2} is a homomorphism that maps each s∈Ss\in S nontrivially. Define G+G^{+} to be the free product G∗⟨y⟩G*{\langle}y{\rangle} and N+N^{+} the normal closure of {s2|s∈S}∪{y2}\{s^{2}|s\in S\}\cup\{y^{2}\}. Extend ρ\rho to a homomorphism ρ+:G+→ℤ2\rho^{+}:G^{+}\to\mathbb{Z}_{2} by mapping yy nontrivially.

Definition 7.2.

𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ){\cal C}(G,S,\rho) is the group Ker​ρ+/N+{\rm Ker}\rho^{+}/N^{+}.

Remark 7.3.

One checks that 𝒞{\cal C} is a covariant functor from the category Core to the category of groups. Objects of 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐞{\bf Core} are 3-tuples (G,S,ρ)(G,S,\rho). Morphisms F:(G1,S1,ρ1)→(G2,S2,ρ2)F:(G_{1},S_{1},\rho_{1})\to(G_{2},S_{2},\rho_{2}) are homomorphisms F:G1→G2F:G_{1}\to G_{2} such that F⁡(N1)⊂N2F(N_{1})\subset N_{2} and ρ2∘F=ρ1\rho_{2}\circ F=\rho_{1}.

Definition 7.4.

Let DD be an oriented virtual link diagram. The standard (Wirtinger) 3-tuple of DD is (πw​i​r​t​(D),S,ρ)(\pi_{wirt}(D),S,\rho), where πw​i​r​t​(D)\pi_{wirt}(D) is the Wirtinger group of the diagram, SS is the set of Wirtinger generators xix_{i}, and ρ:πw​i​r​t​(D)→ℤ2\rho:\pi_{wirt}(D)\to\mathbb{Z}_{2} is the unique homomorphism that maps each xix_{i} nontrivially.

Consider a standard 3-tuple (πw​i​r​t​(D),S,ρ)(\pi_{wirt}(D),S,\rho) of a diagram DD of a virtual link LL. Define L+L^{+} to be the virtual link comprising LL and a distant unknotted component with meridanal generator yy. Any virtual link diagram D+D^{+} of L+L^{+} can be converted to another virtual link diagram of L+L^{+} by a finite sequence of generalized Reidemeister moves. The groups presented by the Wirtinger presentations of equivalent virtual link diagrams are isomorphic by an isomorphism that preserves conjugacy classes of Wirtinger generators. Covariance of the core group functor 𝒞{\cal C} ensures that 𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t​(D),S,ρ){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D),S,\rho) is independent of the diagram of LL. It is also independent of the diagram’s orientation. We will abbreviate the group 𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t​(D),S,ρ){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D),S,\rho) by 𝒞​(πw​i​r​t​(D)){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D)).

Theorem 7.5.

If LL is a virtual link, then 𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t​(D))≅A​C​(D){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D))\cong AC(D).

Proof.

A strictly algebraic proof of this theorem is given in Section 6. Other methods such as the Reidemeister-Schreier method also can be used. Here we give a topological argument, using covering spaces.

Assume that DD is an oriented virtual link diagram for LL with Wirtinger generators xax_{a}, for a∈A⁡(D)a\in A(D), and Wirtinger relators of the form xa1​(c)​xa2​(c)​xa1​(c)−1​xa3​(c)−1x_{a_{1}(c)}x_{a_{2}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{1}(c)}x^{-1}_{a_{3}(c)} at each crossing cc. Consider the standard 2-complex associated to the presentation. It has a single 0-cell bb, oriented 1-cells σa\sigma_{a} corresponding to the Wirtinger generators xax_{a}, and 2-cells τc\tau_{c} with attaching maps described by the relators. Let XX be the complex with an additional 1-cell σy\sigma_{y} to realize the Wirtinger group of D+D^{+}.

Let X~\widetilde{X} be the 2-fold covering space with fundamental group Ker​ρ+{\rm Ker}\ \rho^{+}. It has a lifted complex structure consisting of 0-cells b~,b~′\tilde{b},\tilde{b}^{\prime}; oriented 1-cells σ~a,σ~y\tilde{\sigma}_{a},\tilde{\sigma}_{y} (resp. σ~a′,σ~y′\tilde{\sigma}^{\prime}_{a},\tilde{\sigma}^{\prime}_{y}) from b~\tilde{b} to b~′\tilde{b}^{\prime} (resp. from b~′\tilde{b}^{\prime} to b~\tilde{b}); 2-cells τ~c\tilde{\tau}_{c} (resp. τ~c′\tilde{\tau}^{\prime}_{c}) that are lifts of the τc\tau_{c} with boundaries based at b~\tilde{b} (resp. b~′\tilde{b}^{\prime}). The fundamental group π1​(X~,b~)\pi_{1}(\widetilde{X},\tilde{b}) is generated by the homotopy classes of closed paths based at b~\tilde{b}, the lifts of closed paths in XX based at bb of even word-length.

For each 1-cell σ\sigma in XX attach a 2-cell to X~\widetilde{X} along the closed path σ~​σ~′\tilde{\sigma}\tilde{\sigma}^{\prime}. Denote the new cell complex by X^\widehat{X}. Then the normal subgroup in π1​(X~,b~)\pi_{1}(\widetilde{X},\tilde{b}) generated by the classes of these closed paths is the subgroup N+N^{+} of Definition 7.2. Hence π1​(X^,b~)≅𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t​(D))\pi_{1}(\widehat{X},\tilde{b})\cong{\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D)).

We complete the proof by showing that π1​(X^,b~)\pi_{1}(\widehat{X},\tilde{b}) is isomorphic to A​C​(D)AC(D). To do this, contract the closed path σ~y​σ~y′\tilde{\sigma}_{y}\tilde{\sigma}^{\prime}_{y} together with its bounding 2-cell, identifying b~′\tilde{b}^{\prime} with b~\tilde{b} and converting all remaining 1-cells in X^\widehat{X} to oriented loops based at b~\tilde{b}. We abuse notation by denoting the converted 1-cells (now loops) by the same symbols as before. Contracting σ~y​σ~y′\tilde{\sigma}_{y}\tilde{\sigma}^{\prime}_{y} and the bounding 2-cell preserves the homotopy type and hence the fundamental group of the complex X^\widehat{X}.

We denote the homotopy class of a based oriented closed path with square brackets [⋅][\ \cdot\ ]. Note that [σ~a′]=[σ~a]−1[\tilde{\sigma}^{\prime}_{a}]=[\tilde{\sigma}_{a}]^{-1}. The boundaries of the remaining 2-cells τ~c,τ~c′\tilde{\tau}_{c},\tilde{\tau}_{c}^{\prime} can be read as σ~a1​(c)​σ~a2​(c)−1​σ~a1​(c)​σ~a3​(c)−1\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{1}(c)}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{2}(c)}^{-1}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{1}(c)}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{3}(c)}^{-1} and σ~a1​(c)−1​σ~a2​(c)​σ~a1​(c)−1​σ~a3​(c)\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{1}(c)}^{-1}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{2}(c)}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{1}(c)}^{-1}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{3}(c)}, respectively. (Note the alternating exponents.) The group elements [σ~a1​(c)​σ~a2​(c)−1​σ~a1​(c)​σ~a3​(c)−1][\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{1}(c)}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{2}(c)}^{-1}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{1}(c)}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{3}(c)}^{-1}] and [σ~a1​(c)−1​σ~a2​(c)​σ~a1​(c)−1​σ~a3​(c)]−1[\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{1}(c)}^{-1}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{2}(c)}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{1}(c)}^{-1}\tilde{\sigma}_{a_{3}(c)}]^{-1} are conjugates, so we can ignore the 2-cells τ~j′\tilde{\tau}_{j}^{\prime} without affecting the fundamental group. We obtain the presentation of A​C​(D)AC(D) in Definition 1.1. Hence 𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t​(D))≅π1​(X^,b~){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D))\cong\pi_{1}(\widehat{X},\tilde{b}) is isomorphic to A​C​(D)AC(D). ∎

The above proof suggests an easy procedure for finding a presentation of 𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ){\cal C}(G,S,\rho) when SS generates GG. We describe it next.

Definition 7.6.

If w=gi1ϵ1gi2ϵ2⋯gikϵkw=g_{i_{1}}^{\epsilon_{1}}g_{i_{2}}^{\epsilon_{2}}\cdots g_{i_{k}}^{\epsilon_{k}} is a word in the free group generated by g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} and ϵi=±1\epsilon_{i}=\pm 1, then w~=gi1gi2−1gi3⋯gik(−1)k−1\tilde{w}=g_{i_{1}}g_{i_{2}}^{-1}g_{i_{3}}\cdots g_{i_{k}}^{(-1)^{k-1}} and (w~)′=gi1−1gi2gi3−1⋯gik(−1)k.(\tilde{w})^{\prime}=g_{i_{1}}^{-1}g_{i_{2}}g_{i_{3}}^{-1}\cdots g_{i_{k}}^{(-1)^{k}}.

From the proof of Theorem 7.5 we have:

Proposition 7.7.

Assume that (G,S,ρ)(G,S,\rho) is a triple in the category Core such that GG has a presentation of the form ⟨S;r1,…,rm⟩{\langle}S;r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}{\rangle}. Then 𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ)≅⟨S;r~1,(r~1)′,…,r~m,(r~m)′⟩{\cal C}(G,S,\rho)\cong{\langle}S;\tilde{r}_{1},(\tilde{r}_{1})^{\prime},\ldots,\tilde{r}_{m},(\tilde{r}_{m})^{\prime}{\rangle}.

Remark 7.8.

(1.) A generator s∈Ss\in S of GG should not be confused with the generator s∈𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ)s\in{\cal C}(G,S,\rho). However, the two have a simple relationship. Consider the cover X^\widehat{X} before the 1-cell σy′\sigma^{\prime}_{y} is contracted. A generator s∈Gs\in G is represented by a loop in XX that lifts to directed 1-cell σs\sigma_{s} in X^\widehat{X}. Together with σy′\sigma^{\prime}_{y}, it determines a directed loop in X^\widehat{X} representing s∈𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ)s\in{\cal C}(G,S,\rho).

(2.) It is often the case that the relator (r~i)′(\tilde{r}_{i})^{\prime} is a consequence of r~i\tilde{r}_{i} and hence can be omitted from the presentation in Proposition 7.7.

Corollary 7.9.

A group is isomorphic to the core group of a virtual knot if and only if it has a presentation of the form

⟨x1,…,xn;ui​xi+1~=xi​ui~​(i∈ℤn)⟩,{\langle}x_{1},\ldots,x_{n};\widetilde{u_{i}x_{i+1}}=\widetilde{x_{i}u_{i}}\ (i\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}){\rangle},

where uiu_{i} are arbitrary elements of the free group on x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}.

Proof.

Theorem 2.2 of [17] states that a group is the Wirtinger group of a virtual knot if and only if it has a presentation of the form ⟨x1,…,xn;ui​xi+1=xi​ui​(i∈ℤn)⟩{\langle}x_{1},\ldots,x_{n};u_{i}x_{i+1}=x_{i}u_{i}\ (i\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}){\rangle}, where uiu_{i} are elements of the free group on x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}. Consider the standard core 3-tuple of such a group. Its core group has a presentation

⟨x1,…,xn;ui​xi+1~=xi​ui~,(ui​xi+1~)′=(xi​ui~)′​(i∈ℤn)⟩.{\langle}x_{1},\ldots,x_{n};\widetilde{u_{i}x_{i+1}}=\widetilde{x_{i}u_{i}},(\widetilde{u_{i}x_{i+1}})^{\prime}=(\widetilde{x_{i}u_{i}})^{\prime}\ (i\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}){\rangle}.

It is easily seen that the relations (ui​xi+1~)′=(xi​ui~)′(\widetilde{u_{i}x_{i+1}})^{\prime}=(\widetilde{x_{i}u_{i}})^{\prime} are redundant and so can be omitted. ∎

The Wirtinger group of any classical 2-bridge knot has a simplified presentation ⟨x1,x2;r⟩{\langle}x_{1},x_{2};r{\rangle}, where rr has the form u​x2=x1​uux_{2}=x_{1}u, for some word uu in x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}. Then r~\tilde{r} can be seen to have the form (x1​x2−1)d(x_{1}x_{2}^{-1})^{d}, for some positive integer dd. The following well-known result is immediate.

Corollary 7.10.

The core group of any classical 2-bridge knot is isomorphic to ℤ∗ℤd\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}_{d} for some positive integer dd.

The integer dd in Corollary 7.10 is the determinant of the knot, the order of the fundamental group of its 2-fold branched cyclic cover.

Remark 7.11.

(1.) The proof of Theorem 7.5 suggests alternative ways to compute 𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ){\cal C}(G,S,\rho): In Definition 7.2 we extend GG to G+G^{+} in order to achieve the desired symmetry in the presentation of the core group. However, we can obtain 𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ){\cal C}(G,S,\rho) without extending GG. In the construction of the proof of Theorem 7.5, we can omit the 1-cell yy in the construction of the complex XX. Then instead of contracting the 1-cells σy,σy′\sigma_{y},\sigma^{\prime}_{y} and bounding 2-cell, we can choose any s∈Ss\in S instead of yy, and contract σs∪σs′\sigma_{s}\cup\sigma^{\prime}_{s} and the bounding 2-cell. The group 𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ){\cal C}(G,S,\rho) is isomorphic to ℤ∗Ker​ρ/N\mathbb{Z}*{\rm Ker}\rho/N.

(2.) Since the homomorphism ρ\rho vanishes on the subgroup NN, it induces a well-defined homomorphism ρ¯:G/N→ℤ2\bar{\rho}:G/N\to\mathbb{Z}_{2}. Using the previous remark, we see that 𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ)≅ℤ∗Ker​ρ¯{\cal C}(G,S,\rho)\cong\mathbb{Z}*{\rm Ker}\bar{\rho}.

Proposition 7.12.

Let ℬn{\cal B}_{n} be the nn-string braid group, n≥2n\geq 2, with standard generators b1,…,bn−1b_{1},\dots,b_{n-1}. Let S={b1,…,bn−1}S=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{n-1}\} and ρ:ℬn→ℤ2\rho:{\cal B}_{n}\to\mathbb{Z}_{2} the unique homomorphism mapping each bib_{i} nontrivially. Then 𝒞⁡(ℬn,S,ρ){\cal C}({\cal B}_{n},S,\rho) is isomorphic to ℤ∗An\mathbb{Z}*A_{n}, where AnA_{n} is the alternating group on nn symbols.

Proof.

We recall that ℬn{\cal B}_{n} has presentation

⟨b1,…,bn−1;bi​bi+1​bi=bi+1​bi​bi+1​(∀i),bi​bj=bj​bi​(∀i,j,|i−j|>1)⟩.{\langle}b_{1},\ldots,b_{n-1};b_{i}b_{i+1}b_{i}=b_{i+1}b_{i}b_{i+1}\ (\forall i),b_{i}b_{j}=b_{j}b_{i}\ (\forall i,j,|i-j|>1){\rangle}.

The assignment of each bib_{i} to the transposition si=(i​i+1)s_{i}=(i\ i+1) induces a homomorphism from ℬn{\cal B}_{n} onto the symmetric group SnS_{n}. Its kernel P​ℬnP{\cal B}_{n}, the pure braid group, was shown by Artin to be the normal subgroup of ℬn{\cal B}_{n} generated by b12,…,bn−12b_{1}^{2},\ldots,b_{n-1}^{2}. (See, for example, Chapter 9 of [6].) The kernel of the induced homomorphism ρ¯:ℬn/P​ℬn→ℤ2\bar{\rho}:{\cal B}_{n}/P{\cal B}_{n}\to\mathbb{Z}_{2} is isomorphic to AnA_{n}, the subgroup of SnS_{n} consisting of words of even length in the generators bib_{i}. By Remark 7.11, 𝒞⁡(ℬn,S,ρ){\cal C}({\cal B}_{n},S,\rho) is isomorphic to ℤ∗An\mathbb{Z}*A_{n}.

∎

It is well known that the alternating group has a presentation

An=⟨a1,…,an−2;ai3,(aiaj)2(∀i,j,1≤i≠j≤n−2)⟩A_{n}={\langle}a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-2};a_{i}^{3},(a_{i}a_{j})^{2}\ (\forall i,j,1\leq i\neq j\leq n-2){\rangle}

(see p. 64 of [2]). The procedure from the proof of Theorem 7.5 for finding a presentation of 𝒞⁡(G,S,ρ){\cal C}(G,S,\rho), contracting σbn−1,σbn−1′\sigma_{b_{n-1}},\sigma^{\prime}_{b_{n-1}} and bounding 2-cell, yields a similar presentation for AnA_{n}.

Corollary 7.13.

The alternating group AnA_{n} has presentation

⟨x1,…,xn−1;(xi​xi+1−1)3​(∀i),(xi​xj−1)2​(∀i,j,|i−j|>1),xn−1⟩.{\langle}x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1};(x_{i}x^{-1}_{i+1})^{3}\ (\forall i),(x_{i}x^{-1}_{j})^{2}\ (\forall i,j,|i-j|>1),x_{n-1}{\rangle}.
Example 7.14.

By Corollary 7.13, we obtain

A5≅⟨x1,x2,x3;(x1​x2−1)3,(x2​x3−1)3,x33,(x1​x3−1)2,x12,x22⟩.A_{5}\cong{\langle}x_{1},x_{2},x_{3};(x_{1}x_{2}^{-1})^{3},(x_{2}x_{3}^{-1})^{3},x_{3}^{3},(x_{1}x_{3}^{-1})^{2},x_{1}^{2},x_{2}^{2}{\rangle}.

Using Tietze transformations, we introduce new generators A,B,CA,B,C and defining relations A=x1​x2−1,B=x2​x3−1,C=x3A=x_{1}x_{2}^{-1},B=x_{2}x_{3}^{-1},C=x_{3}. Then

A5≅⟨A,B,C;A3=B3=C3=(AB)2=(BC)2=(ABC)2=1⟩.A_{5}\cong{\langle}A,B,C;A^{3}=B^{3}=C^{3}=(AB)^{2}=(BC)^{2}=(ABC)^{2}=1{\rangle}.

(Here A=s1​s2,B=s2​s3A=s_{1}s_{2},B=s_{2}s_{3} and C=s3​s4C=s_{3}s_{4}.) The presentation of A5A_{5}, originally discovered by J.A. Todd in 1931, appears on p. 125 of [5]:

A5≅⟨V1,V2,V3;V13=V23=V33=(V1V2)2=(V2V3)2=(V3V1)2=1⟩.A_{5}\cong{\langle}V_{1},V_{2},V_{3};V_{1}^{3}=V_{2}^{3}=V_{3}^{3}=(V_{1}V_{2})^{2}=(V_{2}V_{3})^{2}=(V_{3}V_{1})^{2}=1{\rangle}.

8 Coxeter groups

Let M=(mi​j),1≤i,j≤nM=(m_{ij}),1\leq i,j\leq n, be a symmetric n×nn\times n matrix with entries in ℕ∪{∞}{\mathbb{N}}\cup\{\infty\}, such that mi​i=1m_{ii}=1 for all ii and mi​j>1m_{ij}>1 if i≠ji\neq j. The Coxeter group of type MM (see [19]) is the group defined by the presentation

W=⟨s1,…,sn;(si​sj)mi​j​(∀i,mi​j<∞)⟩.W={\langle}s_{1},\ldots,s_{n};(s_{i}s_{j})^{m_{ij}}\ (\forall i,m_{ij}<\infty){\rangle}. (8.1)

Since diagonal entries of MM are equal to 11, each generator sis_{i} satisfies si2=1s_{i}^{2}=1. Consequently, mi​j=2m_{ij}=2 implies that sis_{i} and sjs_{j} commute.

The information of the matrix MM can be encoded by a graph with nn vertices labeled s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n}. There is an edge connecting sis_{i} and sjs_{j} and labeled by mi​jm_{ij} whenever mi​j>2m_{ij}>2. By convention, edges labeled 2 are omitted, while any unlabeled edge is assumed to be labeled 3.

Any Coxeter group WW has a natural associated triple (W,S,ρ)(W,S,\rho), where S={s1,…,sn}S=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\} and ρ:W→Z/2\rho:W\to Z/2 is the unique homomorphism mapping each sis_{i} nontrivially. We will call (W,S,ρ)(W,S,\rho) the standard triple of WW. We denote by 𝒞⁡(W){\cal C}(W) the group determined by the core functor with the standard triple of WW.

Proposition 8.1.

If WW is the Coxeter group of type MM, then 𝒞⁡(W){\cal C}(W) is isomorphic to the free product of ℤ\mathbb{Z} and the kernel of ρ\rho.

Proof.

Since each square si2s_{i}^{2} is trivial in WW, the subgroup SS is trivial. By Remark 2 of 7.11, 𝒞⁡(W,S,ρ){\cal C}(W,S,\rho) is isomorphic to ℤ∗Ker​ρ\mathbb{Z}*{\rm Ker}\rho. ∎

Example 8.2.

The symmetric group SnS_{n} generated by transpositions si=(i​i+1),1≤i<ns_{i}=(i\ i+1),1\leq i<n, is the Coxeter group corresponding to the graph that consists of n−1n-1 vertices joined by n−2n-2 unlabeled edges. Consider the standard triple (Sn,S,ρ)(S_{n},S,\rho). The kernel of ρ\rho is the alternating group AnA_{n}. Hence 𝒞⁡(Sn)≅ℤ∗An{\cal C}(S_{n})\cong\mathbb{Z}*A_{n}. (Compare with Proposition 7.12.)

Example 8.3.

The group of the (2,m)(2,m)-torus link has a presentation πw​i​r​t≅⟨s1,s2;s1s2s1⋯=s2s1s2⋯⟩\pi_{wirt}\cong{\langle}s_{1},s_{2};s_{1}s_{2}s_{1}\cdots=s_{2}s_{1}s_{2}\cdots{\rangle}, where each side of the relation has length mm. Both s1s_{1} and s2s_{2} are Wirtinger generators, and in fact the presentation is obtained from a Wirtinger presentation by applying Tietze transformations. Consider the standard triple (πw​i​r​t,S,ρ)(\pi_{wirt},S,\rho). Then the quotient group πw​i​r​t/N\pi_{wirt}/N has presentation ⟨s1,s2;s12,s22,(s1​s2)m⟩{\langle}s_{1},s_{2};s_{1}^{2},s_{2}^{2},(s_{1}s_{2})^{m}{\rangle}. This is a Coxeter group corresponding to the graph consisting of two vertices joined by a single edge labeled mm.

Proposition 7.7 can be used to see that 𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}) has presentation ⟨s1,s2;(s1​s2−1)m⟩{\langle}s_{1},s_{2};(s_{1}s_{2}^{-1})^{m}{\rangle}. Let U=s1​s2−1U=s_{1}s_{2}^{-1}. Then Tietze transformations convert the presentation to ⟨s1,U;Um⟩≅ℤ∗ℤm{\langle}s_{1},U;U^{m}{\rangle}\cong\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}_{m}.

Example 8.4.

Consider the Coxeter group W≅⟨s1,s2,s3;s12,s22,s32,(s1​s2)3,(s2​s3)3,(s3​s1)3⟩W\cong{\langle}s_{1},s_{2},s_{3};s_{1}^{2},s_{2}^{2},s_{3}^{2},(s_{1}s_{2})^{3},(s_{2}s_{3})^{3},(s_{3}s_{1})^{3}{\rangle} corresponding to the graph consisting of a triangle with unlabeled edges. Consider the standard triple (W,S,ρ)(W,S,\rho). The method of the proof of Theorem 7.5 can be used to see that 𝒞⁡(W){\cal C}(W) has presentation ⟨s1,s2,s3;(s1​s2−1)3,(s2​s3−1)3,(s3​s1−1)3⟩{\langle}s_{1},s_{2},s_{3};(s_{1}s_{2}^{-1})^{3},(s_{2}s_{3}^{-1})^{3},(s_{3}s_{1}^{-1})^{3}{\rangle}. Let U=s1​s2−1U=s_{1}s_{2}^{-1} and V=s2​s3−1V=s_{2}s_{3}^{-1}. Then Tietze transformations convert the presentation to ⟨s1,U,V;U3,V3,(U​V)3⟩≅ℤ∗⟨U,V;U3,V3,(U​V)3⟩{\langle}s_{1},U,V;U^{3},V^{3},(UV)^{3}{\rangle}\cong\mathbb{Z}*{\langle}U,V;U^{3},V^{3},(UV)^{3}{\rangle}.

The group WW is the plane crystallographic (“wallpaper”) group p31m while 𝒞⁡(W){\cal C}(W) is the free product of ℤ\mathbb{Z} and the index-2 subgroup p3 of p31m (see pp. 48–49 of [5]).

9 Dehn core groups from Dehn groups

We return our attention to the Dehn group of a virtual link diagram DD and its relationship to the region core group R​C​(D)RC(D).

Recall that DD corresponds to an abstract link diagram, a classical link diagram on a surface Σ{\Sigma} for which the underlying 4-valent graph is a deformation retract. By attaching 2-disks along the boundary of the surface we obtain a link diagram in a closed surface 𝒮{\cal S}. The regions of the abstract link diagram are preserved (although they are enlarged by the added disks), and so we can find the presentation of πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) from the diagram D⊂𝒮D\subset{\cal S}. It is straightforward to see that πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) is unchanged by Reidemeister moves in 𝒮{\cal S} as well as surface automorphisms. If we thicken 𝒮{\cal S}, regarding it as 𝒮×{0}⊂𝒮×[−1,1]{\cal S}\times\{0\}\subset{\cal S}\times[-1,1], then DD describes a link L⊂𝒮×[−1,1]L\subset{\cal S}\times[-1,1], and πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) is an invariant of LL up to ambient isotopy and automorphisms of 𝒮×[−1,1]{\cal S}\times[-1,1]. Conversely, it is straightforward to see that any link LL in a thickened surface 𝒮×[−1,1]{\cal S}\times[-1,1] arises in the above manner from a diagram D⊂𝒮D\subset{\cal S}. Henceforth surfaces 𝒮{\cal S} are assumed to be closed, connected and orientable.

A link diagram D⊂𝒮D\subset{\cal S} is checkerboard colorable if and only if LL represents the trivial element in the mod-2 homology of 𝒮×[−1,1]{\cal S}\times[-1,1]. (This can be proved by observing that the intersection of DD with each boundary arc of a fundamental region Δ{\Delta} of 𝒮{\cal S} has an even number of points if and only if DD is checkerboard colorable.) Recall that πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) has Dehn generators χS\chi_{S} corresponding to shaded regions SS together with Dehn generators χU\chi_{U} corresponding to unshaded regions UU, with a single shaded generator χS0\chi_{S_{0}} set equal to the identity. Lemma 2.3 and Corollary 2.4 tell us that it does not matter which shaded region is chosen as S0S_{0}. (One can equally well chose the region to be unshaded.) When DD is checkerboard colorable, there is a unique homomorphism ρ:πd​e​h​n​(D)→ℤ2\rho:\pi_{dehn}(D)\to\mathbb{Z}_{2} mapping each χS\chi_{S} to 0 and each χU\chi_{U} to 1.

Each arc of DD determines elements of the form χU​χS−1\chi_{U}\chi_{S}^{-1}, with UU on one side of the arc and SS on the other side (at the same point). We will refer to them as arc elements of πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D). We define a standard Dehn 3-tuple of DD to be (πd​e​h​n​(D),S,ρ)(\pi_{dehn}(D),S,\rho), where SS is the set of arc elements. Let ρ:πd​e​h​n​(D)→ℤ2\rho:\pi_{dehn}(D)\to\mathbb{Z}_{2} be the homomorphism described above, sending each χS\chi_{S} to 0 and χU\chi_{U} to 1. Note that the 3-tuple depends on the choice of a generator that we set equal to the identity in the definition of the Dehn group, a choice that determines the homomorphism ρ\rho. When the choice of generator is clear, we refer to (πd​e​h​n​(D),S,ρ)(\pi_{dehn}(D),S,\rho) as the standard Dehn 3-tuple and shorten the notation 𝒞⁡(πd​e​h​n​(D),S,ρ){\cal C}(\pi_{dehn}(D),S,\rho) to 𝒞​(πd​e​h​n​(D)){\cal C}(\pi_{dehn}(D)).

Assume that χS0\chi_{S_{0}} is the generator set equal to the identity element in the definition of the Dehn group. By Proposition 2.6, the element χS0\chi_{S_{0}} generates an infinite cyclic free factor of R​C​(D)RC(D). The remaining factor, R​C0​(D)RC^{0}(D), is isomorphic to R​C​(D)/⟨χS0⟩RC(D)/{\langle}\chi_{S_{0}}{\rangle} and has generators in one-to-one correspondence with those of πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D). By Lemma 2.5 and Proposition 2.6, up to isomorphism R​C0​(D)RC^{0}(D) does not depend on the particular region S0S_{0}.

A fundamental region Δ{\Delta} of a genus-gg surface 𝒮{\cal S} has 4​g4g boundary arcs, identified in pairs in the usual way. Assume that the diagram DD is oriented. Reading along an arc β\beta in either direction, let wβ=xai1ϵ1​…​xairϵr∈πw​i​r​t​(D)w_{\beta}=x_{a_{i_{1}}}^{\epsilon_{1}}\ldots x_{a_{i_{r}}}^{\epsilon_{r}}\in\pi_{wirt}(D), where ai1,…,aira_{i_{1}},\ldots,a_{i_{r}} are the arcs of DD that are successively encountered, and ϵi=ai⋅β\epsilon_{i}=a_{i}\cdot\beta is the oriented intersection number computed in 𝒮{\cal S}. Denote by W⁡(Δ)W({\Delta}) the normal subgroup of πw​i​r​t​(D)\pi_{wirt}(D) generated by the set of elements wβw_{\beta}, with β\beta ranging over the boundary arcs of Δ{\Delta}. By Theorem 3.2.2 of [3] (also Theorem 4.4 of [18]), πw​i​r​t​(D)/W​(Δ)\pi_{wirt}(D)/W({\Delta}) is isomorphic to πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D). The isomorphism in [18] identifies Wirtinger generators with the arc elements or their inverses in the Dehn group.

Remark 9.1.

Reading along β\beta in an opposite direction produces the inverse element. Hence the direction that we choose is unimportant. Also, if β′\beta^{\prime} and β\beta are identified in the surface, then ωβ\omega_{\beta} is equal to ωβ′\omega_{\beta^{\prime}} or ωβ′−1\omega^{-1}_{\beta^{\prime}}. Therefore, we need consider only 2​g2g boundary arcs.

Let A​C​(Δ)AC({\Delta}) be the normal subgroup of A​C​(D)AC(D) generated by the elements ωβ=gai1​gai2−1​gai3​…​gair−1\omega_{\beta}=g_{a_{i_{1}}}g_{a_{i_{2}}}^{-1}g_{a_{i_{3}}}\ldots g_{a_{i_{r}}}^{-1} and ωβ′=gai1−1​gai2​gai3−1​…​gair\omega^{\prime}_{\beta}=g_{a_{i_{1}}}^{-1}g_{a_{i_{2}}}g_{a_{i_{3}}}^{-1}\ldots g_{a_{i_{r}}}, with β\beta ranging over the boundary arcs of Δ{\Delta}.

The following generalizes Theorem 2.6.

Theorem 9.2.

If DD is a checkerboard colorable link diagram in a surface 𝒮{\cal S} with fundamental region Δ{\Delta}, then A​C​(D)/A​C​(Δ)≅R​C0​(D)AC(D)/AC({\Delta})\cong RC^{0}(D).

Proof.

Recall from Section 2 that we have a function A⁡(D)A(D) to R​C​(D)RC(D) sending aa to γU​γS−1{\gamma}_{U}{\gamma}_{S}^{-1}, where UU (resp. SS) is the unshaded (resp. shaded) region incident at some point of the arc aa. Moreover, the function determines a surjection f:A​C​(D)→R​C0​(D)f:AC(D)\to RC^{0}(D). It is clear that ff vanishes on the subgroup A​C​(Δ)AC({\Delta}), and hence induces a homomorphism f¯:A​C​(D)/A​C​(Δ)→R​C0​(D)\bar{f}:AC(D)/AC({\Delta})\to RC^{0}(D).

We have also a map h:R​C0​(D)→A​C​(D)/A​C​(Δ)h:RC^{0}(D)\to AC(D)/AC({\Delta}) sending the generator γR{\gamma}_{R} of any region of DD to an element of A​C​(D)AC(D). We review the process. Recall we defined χS0∈πd​e​h​n​(D)\chi_{S_{0}}\in\pi_{dehn}(D) to be trivial in the definition of the Dehn group. Choose a path from S0S_{0} to RR, crossing the arcs of DD transversely and avoiding crossings. Suppose that a0,a1,…,ama_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{m} are the arcs that we cross successively. If RR is shaded, then h(γR)=gam−1gam−1gam−2−1⋯ga0h({\gamma}_{R})=g_{a_{m}}^{-1}g_{a_{m-1}}g_{a_{m-2}}^{-1}\cdots g_{a_{0}}. If RR is unshaded then h(γR)=gamgam−1−1gam−2⋯ga0h({\gamma}_{R})=g_{a_{m}}g_{a_{m-1}}^{-1}g_{a_{m-2}}\cdots g_{a_{0}}.

The process we have described is a sort of integration, accumulating generators of A​C​(D)AC(D) or their inverse each time we cross an arc. We can apply it to a path from one region, with an initial value, to another. We will refer to the final value that we obtain as the “return value.” For example, if the path is a loop around a crossing of DD, then one checks easily that the return value is equal to the initial value. We can see why h⁡(γR)h({\gamma}_{R}) is independent of the choice of path from S0S_{0} to RR, modulo A​C​(Δ)AC({\Delta}), by considering an arbitrary closed path beginning and ending in S0S_{0}. Such a loop can be moved past any crossing without changing its return value. We can deform the loop to the boundary of Δ{\Delta}, an embedded bouquet of loops in 𝒮{\cal S}. Reading as above along any closed boundary arc returns the initial value modulo the subgroup A​C​(Δ)AC({\Delta}). Hence the closed path with trivial initial value also returns the trivial value in the quotient A​C​(D)/A​C​(Δ)AC(D)/AC({\Delta}).

Finally, one checks as in Section 2 that the maps ff and hh are inverses of each other. ∎

Remark 9.3.

The definition of the map hh depends on the region S0S_{0} for which χS0\chi_{S_{0}} is the identity. For the following, we will choose S0S_{0} also to be the region for which gS0g_{S_{0}} is the identity in the definition of the Dehn group πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D).

Theorem 9.4.

If DD is a checkerboard colorable diagram in a surface, then 𝒞⁡(πd​e​h​n​(D))≅R​C0​(D){\cal C}(\pi_{dehn}(D))\cong RC^{0}(D).

Proof.

Provide an orientation for DD. The standard Wirtinger 3-tuple (πw​i​r​t​(D),S,ρ)(\pi_{wirt}(D),S,\rho) induces a 3-tuple (πw​i​r​t​(D)/W⁡(Δ),S¯,ρ¯)(\pi_{wirt}(D)/W({\Delta}),\bar{S},\bar{\rho}), with S¯\bar{S} and ρ¯\bar{\rho} defined naturally. Since an isomorphism between πw​i​r​t​(D)/W​(Δ)\pi_{wirt}(D)/W({\Delta}) and πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) matches Wirtinger generators with arc elements of πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) or their inverses, (πw​i​r​t​(D)/W⁡(Δ),S¯,ρ¯)(\pi_{wirt}(D)/W({\Delta}),\bar{S},\bar{\rho}) is isomorphic in the category Core to the standard Dehn 3-tuple. Hence it suffices to prove that 𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t​(D)/W⁡(Δ),S¯,ρ¯){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D)/W({\Delta}),\bar{S},\bar{\rho}) is isomorphic to R​C0​(D)RC^{0}(D).

The construction in the proof of Theorem 7.5 yields a presentation of 𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t​(D)/W⁡(Δ),S¯,ρ¯){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D)/W({\Delta}),\bar{S},\bar{\rho}). The cover X^\widehat{X} that we produce with fundamental group 𝒞​(πw​i​r​t​(D)){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D)) acquires extra 2-cells corresponding to the generators of W⁡(Δ)W({\Delta}). By Theorem 7.5, 𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t​(D))≅A​C​(D){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D))\cong AC(D), and the boundaries of the extra 2-cells generate A​C​(Δ)AC({\Delta}). Hence OPEN𝒞⁡(πw​i​r​t​(D)/W⁡(Δ),N¯,ρ¯))≅A​C​(D)/A​C​(Δ){\cal C}(\pi_{wirt}(D)/W({\Delta}),\bar{N},\bar{\rho}))\cong AC(D)/AC({\Delta}). By Theorem 9.2, the latter group is R​C0​(D).RC^{0}(D). ∎

Example 9.5.

The diagram DD below represents a knot in a thickened torus. The Wirtinger group πw​i​r​t​(D)\pi_{wirt}(D) has presentation

⟨a,b,c;a​b−1​a=b​a​b−1,d−1​b​d=b−1​d​b,b−1​d​b​a−1​b−1​d​b​a​b−1​d−1​b​a−1⟩.{\langle}a,b,c;ab^{-1}a=bab^{-1},d^{-1}bd=b^{-1}db,b^{-1}dba^{-1}b^{-1}dbab^{-1}d^{-1}ba^{-1}{\rangle}. (9.1)

Adding the relations a=da=d and b=cb=c, read along the boundary of the fundamental region, produces a presentation for the Dehn group πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D):

⟨a,b;a​b​a=b​a​b,a2=b2⟩.{\langle}a,b;aba=bab,a^{2}=b^{2}{\rangle}. (9.2)

A presentation for πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) can also be calculated directly from the diagram:

⟨A,B;A​B​A=B​A​B,A2=B2⟩.{\langle}A,B;ABA=BAB,A^{2}=B^{2}{\rangle}. (9.3)

The group presented can be seen to be the semidirect product of ℤ\mathbb{Z} acting nontrivially on ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3}. Applying Proposition 7.7 to the presentation (9.1) and using the substitutions U=b​d−1,V=b​a−1U=bd^{-1},V=ba^{-1}, we obtain the following presentation for A​C​(D)AC(D):

⟨b,U,V;U3,V3,(U​V)3⟩≅ℤ∗⟨U,V;U3,V3,(U​V)3⟩.{\langle}b,U,V;U^{3},V^{3},(UV)^{3}{\rangle}\cong\mathbb{Z}*{\langle}U,V;U^{3},V^{3},(UV)^{3}{\rangle}.

The second free factor is the plane crystallographic (“wallpaper”) group p3 (see for example [5], page 48). We apply Theorem 9.2 and Proposition 7.7 to the presentation (9.2) to obtain a presentation of R​C0​(D)RC^{0}(D):

⟨a,b;(a​b−1)3⟩≅ℤ∗ℤ3.{\langle}a,b;(ab^{-1})^{3}{\rangle}\cong\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}_{3}.

Hence R​C​(D)≅ℤ∗ℤ∗ℤ3RC(D)\cong\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}_{3}. Alternatively, one can compute a presentation of R​C​(D)RC(D) directly from presentation (9.3):

⟨A,B,C;(B​A−1)3⟩.{\langle}A,B,C;(BA^{-1})^{3}{\rangle}.

We finish with the observation that the conclusion of Theorem 7.5 does not hold in general for diagrams that are not checkerboard colorable. One can easily verify that for the diagram in the figure below the Dehn group πd​e​h​n​(D)\pi_{dehn}(D) is trivial and hence so is 𝒞​(πd​e​h​n​(D)){\cal C}(\pi_{dehn}(D)). However, R​C0​(D)RC^{0}(D) is cyclic of order 3.
